title: Inference headroom, SLOs, KV warmup & reserved GPU runbook - Peregrine Labs
summary: Deep technical session to align on capacity headroom targets, queueing model for spike protection, KV-cache warmup behavior, quantization tradeoffs, and a runbook for reserved GPU fallback during high-load windows. Agreed next steps include Redwood sending a tailored runbook, a short benchmark template, and Peregrine scheduling a pilot for end of month.

transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-08-05 15:00 UTC | Duration: 72m | Recording: on

Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Ava (Redwood SE), Liam (CTO Peregrine), Sofia (MLOps), Dev (Infra), Rachel (Product)

Summary (auto): align on headroom and fallback patterns for reserved capacity; define runbook for KV warmup and queueing behavior.

00:00:03 Jordan: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I'll kick us off. we have Ava from our infra team and we'll aim to cover headroom targets, queueing/backpressure model, and the reserved GPU failover runbook.
00:00:18 Liam: Sounds good, we only have about 70 minutes so yeah, want to get to the runbook part cause we have an exec review friday.
00:00:28 Ava: Quick note - I may reference some internal kernel timings and our kv-cache warm up heuristics, if anything is unclear stop me.
00:00:39 Sofia: Perfect, we ran into a weird thing last week where cold-starts spiked 30% of p99s during a marketing blast so that is the top pain.

00:01:05 Jordan: Got it. before we dive, can you share your target SLOs? what P95/P99 and error budgets are you trying to hold?
00:01:18 Liam: We want 250ms P95 for chat endpoints and p99 under 1.5 seconds for typical 512-token outputs. error budget is small, like 0.5% monthly.
00:01:34 Ava: Ok that's fairly tight. two knobs: reserved GPUs to absorb sustained load, and headroom buffers for spikes plus a short-lived queueing tier for graceful degradation.
00:01:48 Dev: Quick clarifying q - reserved GPUs would be on your Dedicated offering with VPC peering, correct? we need to know ip ranges and security.
00:01:59 Jordan: Yes reserved = Dedicated. We do VPC peering or private link; we'll share network ranges. Jordan: we'll include the egress and KMS notes in the runbook.

00:02:25 Ava: on the queueing model — we recommend a two-tier approach: immediate path (latency SLOs) and a short worker queue for best-effort requests with TTL 8-12s depending on the UA. if queue length grows past N we trigger a reserved-pool scale or fallback to a cheaper quantized variant.
00:02:49 Sofia: when you say fallback to cheaper variant — that's quantized model with lower memory right? what is the observed p99 delta?
00:03:01 Ava: good q — in our tests 4-bit quantized variants on A100-ish or H100 quant paths can reduce per-token cost by ~1.6-2x and throughput increases a bit, but p99 latency can be slightly worse because of kernel differences, it's workload dependent. for short outputs 1-2x improvement cost with p99 up ~5-15% in worst cases.
00:03:27 Rachel: So if we have a marketing blast and need rough answers fast then fallback to quantized is ok? product says yes but we need to understand quality regressions.
00:03:40 Ava: Exactly. that's why we recommend a staged fallback: first increase concurrency on reserved pool, then spill to cached prefixes or local KV, then quantized, finally rate-limit.

00:04:05 Dev: about KV warmup: we saw cold KV misses cause an extra 120ms on average initially. is that consistent with your benchmarks?
00:04:17 Ava: That aligns. KV cache warmup varies. if your traffic has a large tail of unique prompts, warmup hurts. our heuristics: pre-warm high-frequency prefixes and maintain a small warmup-eviction buffer that is sticky across bursts. warmup script in the repo does simulated prefetch.
00:04:39 Liam: do you do proactive kv-warmup on reserved pools during pre-scheduled campaigns? like a runbook entry?
00:04:47 Jordan: yes we do a pre-warm step in the runbook: when you expect a campaign we recommend a warm-up window 15-45 minutes prior depending on history, pumping representative prefixes at production-concurrency.

00:05:12 Ava: important nuance: continuous batching and kv cache interplay. If you start many concurrent short requests, batching increases throughput but can add head-of-line p99 noise at small qps spikes. The runbook recommends batch-size caps per model per pool.
00:05:31 Sofia: what's the recommended batch cap for 512-token Llama2-like workloads?
00:05:38 Ava: empirically for 512 tokens on our tuned kernels: batch cap 8-16 for latency-sensitive, 32+ for throughput-optimized. with quantization you can push caps higher but watch memory.

00:06:05 Dev: queueing theory question — do you model spikes as poisson or heavier tail? our bursts are marketing blasts which look like heavy-tail with short time correlation.
00:06:17 Ava: we use a mix — base model is a compound poisson with burstiness factor; for real campaigns we recommend using empirical traces and running a simulation (we can provide a simulator). heavy-tail means you should plan for longer headroom and quicker fallback steps.
00:06:36 Jordan: we'll ask for your 7-day trace to run exactly that sim and provide a recommended reserved capacity and headroom percentage.

00:06:52 Liam: what headroom percent do you usually recommend? we dont want to overpay.
00:06:58 Ava: start conservative: 25-40% headroom above your peak 95th percentile qps for the paid window. if you can commit to shorter warmup windows and have stronger prefix caching, you can push that down to 10-15%. the runbook will show a cost tradeoff table.

00:07:22 Rachel: cost tradeoffs matter — can you show the delta between a larger reserved pool vs autoscale + quantized spill? execs want a monthly cost estimate.
00:07:31 Jordan: yes we'll include three scenarios in the spreadsheet: reserved-heavy, hybrid (reserved + autoscale with burst), and minimal reserved + aggressive quantized fallback.

00:07:47 Ava: also watch tail latency introduced by preemption/eviction on overloaded GPUs. reserved pools reduce eviction noise; ephemeral pools for burst are cheaper but risk preemption and kv-state loss.
00:08:03 Dev: question about state — our service pins some session KV per user. if an ephemeral preemptible instance gets killed do you persist KV to remote store or is it lost?
00:08:16 Ava: by default ephemeral pools rely on remote durable KV for long-term state; local KV is warm cache only. our recommended pattern: critical session state writes back to durable store asynchronously and keep only best-effort local KV. the runbook includes an example pipeline.

00:08:42 Liam: ok good. can you walk through a concrete failover scenario step-by-step? like marketing blast triggers | thresholds | runbook actions.
00:08:53 Ava: sure. step 1: monitor P95 and queue length. threshold A: P95 > 250ms and queue length > 30 for 30s -> trigger autoscale up reserved pool by X nodes. step 2: if scale up doesn't reduce p99 within 45s, activate spill to quantized model variant with sticky session routing. step 3: if p99 still bad, start shedding best-effort routes (background summarizers) and throttle new sessions. step 4: if sustained beyond 5 minutes, page on-call and route traffic to cross-region fallback.
00:09:33 Sofia: those thresholds feel tight; can we tune them?
00:09:37 Ava: absolutely, they are templates. the runbook will include tuned thresholds based on your trace.

00:09:52 Jordan: quick aside on metrics - we recommend instrumentation at token-level for latency, and route-level breakdowns, also KV hit/miss rates. those feed the warmup heuristics.
00:10:07 Dev: token-level metrics? that seems heavy.
00:10:11 Ava: it's lightweight if you sample or aggregate at 1s windows. we provide a Fluentd exporter and metric hooks.

00:10:27 Liam: about quantization — we dont want hallucination regressions. can Redwood provide quality regressions metrics when we run the quantized fallback?
00:10:36 Ava: yes, our Optimize team runs evals on prompt sets and outputs delta metrics like ROUGE/BLEU or embedding-sim similarity for LLM outputs. we'll include a QA checklist in the runbook to check for semantic drift before enabling fallback for critical routes.

00:10:58 Rachel: VPC/on-prem: we plan to run private for PHI. any constraints on warmup traffic across peered network? network egress cost?
00:11:09 Jordan: with VPC peering warmup traffic flows securely but egress costs vary across clouds. we'll add cost estimates and options to pre-warm via a local ramp tool inside your VPC to avoid cross-region egress.

00:11:26 Dev: KMS question — if we use customer-managed keys will that add latency during token decrypt?
00:11:34 Ava: minor at init time only — per-request decrypts are cached. initial cold-starts can add ~30-60ms depending on KMS region. include a note to cache keys in our sidecar on private deployments.

00:11:52 Liam: let's shift to benchmarks — what do you need from us to run a realistic benchmark that reflects our spikes?
00:11:59 Ava: your 7-day qps trace with token-length distribution, a set of 50 representative prompts for each route, and network constraints (VPC peering, region). with that we run two sims: one where we load-add traffic to 2x peak and one with injected heavy-tail spikes.
00:12:18 Jordan: and we'll demonstrate a small pilot: 24-48 hour pilot using a dedicated test pool with pre-warm to show p95/p99 under your expected traffic.

00:12:30 Sofia: acceptable. we can export logs; should we sanitize anything?
00:12:34 Dev: yes remove PII; we'll share aggregated histograms.

00:12:40 Ava: good. small technical note on KV cache warmup strategies: prefer frequency-based prefetch over LRU for campaign windows; sticky TTLs and a warmup headroom of 2-3x expected synthetic clients works well.
00:12:56 Liam: frequency-based prefetch meaning you analyze last 24-48 hours and pre-seed the cache?
00:13:01 Ava: exactly. identify top prefixes and pre-populate them on the reserved pool. we provide scripts for that.

00:13:17 Jordan: alright let's deep dive quick on the math for headroom and queueing. Ava?
00:13:22 Ava: simple model: required_capacity = ceil(peak_qps * mean_latency / concurrency_efficiency). headroom = factor * required_capacity. factor derived from burst kurtosis. for heavy tail we choose factor 1.25-1.4. queue ttl chosen such that expected wait < SLO slack. we can share the sim outputs.
00:13:47 Dev: you mentioned concurrency efficiency. what's typical for 512-token runs?
00:13:52 Ava: on our serving kernels concurrency efficiency ~0.7 for latency-first configs, ~0.9 for throughput-first. that is used to scale raw GPU counts.
00:14:07 Liam: ok. now on reserved GPU failover steps - can we have a short runbook outline live?
00:14:13 Jordan: yes I'll read the outline and we can capture gaps. step 0: pre-campaign checklist (kv pre-seed, warmup script, network checks, KMS warmed). step 1: monitoring thresholds (P95 > threshold, queue > threshold). step 2: autoscale/reserved add nodes (with fastest path and slower path). step 3: spill to quantized variant. step 4: shed non-critical routes. step 5: cross-region fallback. step 6: post-mortem and warmup retention adjustments.
00:14:51 Sofia: good. one specific gap: session affinity during spill — will user sessions be sticky to preserve context?
00:14:59 Ava: yes we'll use a sticky routing key at the proxy layer to keep session stickiness to the new variant if possible; otherwise, we attach a continuity token and reconstruct KV on first request. runbook notes steps.

00:15:20 Dev: about eviction behavior on reserved nodes — if we add nodes quickly will eviction cause KV churn causing more cold misses?
00:15:29 Ava: adding nodes is generally good because it increases KV capacity; eviction problems happen when you remove nodes. the runbook recommends ramp-down grace windows and draining strategies to persist hot KV keys.
00:15:45 Liam: how long to warm up a new reserved node's KV state?
00:15:50 Ava: depends on hotspots but with targeted pre-seeding can be 5-10 minutes for top prefixes; full tail warmup can be hours depending on unique prompts.

00:16:10 Jordan: okay we have a few minutes left, are there other concerns?
00:16:13 Sofia: compliance around logs — will Redwood redact PII in debug traces? we need SOC2 evidence.
00:16:21 Jordan: yes we can provide SOC2/ISO docs and show redaction steps; we'll include a short compliance checklist in the runbook.

00:16:35 Dev: one more nit — our infra team needs the exact ip ranges and docker images used for private deploy.
00:16:42 Jordan: we'll attach those in the follow-up; images and digests included.

00:16:50 Ava: and a note on quantization CI — before enabling fallback in prod, run a small A/B with held-out prompts and an automated regressions check. we can hook into your CI to gate it.
00:17:03 Rachel: ok that's useful. question: do you support per-route fallback policies so marketing pages can use aggressive fallback while billing uses stricter rules?
00:17:13 Ava: yes per-route routing policies are supported; we can set different thresholds and model variants per route.

00:17:27 Jordan: resolution: we'll produce runbook, cost spreadsheet, benchmark template, and warmup scripts. We'll run a pilot after Pernrgrine shares traces.

00:17:40 Liam: typo - Peregrine. yes. appreciate it. last ask: can you include a simple SLA language sample for reserved pools for our procurement?
00:17:50 Jordan: yes procurement sample SLA included.

00:18:00 -- Transcript continues in more detail with Q&A and noise --

00:30:12 Ava: [deep dive] kernel note: for certain attention-kernel shapes our runtime will switch to chunked attention which improves memory locality but can increase per-token latency var; toggles in config.
00:31:00 Dev: is chunked attention used by default?
00:31:04 Ava: only when memory pressure triggers it or when sequence length crosses a threshold. you'll see that in profile.

00:34:20 Sofia: during the pilot can we measure embedding route separately? those have different token patterns.
00:34:27 Ava: yes split routes; embeddings often use different model family and batching characteristics.

00:42:10 Jordan: we need to capture estimated cost delta numbers now? quick sketch - reserved pool with X GPUs estimated monthly cost Y, hybrid 30% lower for baseline but higher variance. exact numbers in spreadsheet.

00:51:40 Ava: small implementation note: when draining nodes we serialize KV to remote store in batches to avoid network spikes; runbook recommends throttle windows.

01:03:05 Liam: what about security scanning for the private docker images? we must run our scanner.
01:03:12 Jordan: images are signed and you can run your scanner; we'll provide image digests.

01:12:30 Ava: final note: test your canary with synthetic spike test at 2x expected peak; that reveals queueing thresholds and eviction policies.
01:12:45 Jordan: great. thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the docs and schedule the benchmark.

01:13:00 Meeting end.

Post-meeting notes: links shared - Runbook draft (internal): https://redwood.work/runbooks/peregrine-kv-reserved-draft (view-only); Benchmark template: https://redwood.work/benchmarks/template-v2 (shared); Cost model spreadsheet link: https://redwood.work/costs/peregrine-estimate.xlsx (request access)
